claims.text: CoCrFeMnNi is a single-phase high-entropy alloy in the system under consideration.
CoCrFeMnNi can exhibit inverse Hall-Petch behavior in an inert or ultra-high-vacuum environment.
The coarse-grained baseline follows classical Hall-Petch behavior during moderate grain refinement.
Thermomechanical processing can refine CoCrFeMnNi to sub-micron grains while retaining a single-phase solid solution.
An inert environment mitigates oxidation-related effects during mechanical testing.
Grain refinement increases the fraction of grain boundaries susceptible to stress-induced amorphization.
Deformation produces a dynamically amorphized, ultra-nanocrystalline layer at grain boundaries.
A dynamic-amorphization model predicts grain-size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime.
The amorphous interfacial layer raises the barrier for dislocation nucleation.
Dynamic grain-boundary amorphization increases lattice friction during dislocation activity.
Dynamic grain-boundary amorphization governs hardness in refined CoCrFeMnNi.
Dynamic grain-boundary amorphization governs yield strength in refined CoCrFeMnNi.
The ultrafine-grained sample will have greater hardness than the coarse-grained baseline.
The ultrafine-grained sample will have greater yield strength than the coarse-grained baseline.
Below a critical grain size, strength ceases to scale linearly with decreasing grain size because dynamic amorphization begins.
The proposed mechanism applies generally to single-phase, equiatomic high-entropy alloys at room temperature in inert environments.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis labels the below-threshold behavior as inverse Hall-Petch while also predicting that further grain refinement causes increased lattice friction and a non-linear increase in hardness and yield strength. Inverse Hall-Petch behavior conventionally denotes decreasing strength with further grain-size reduction, so the predicted direction is internally inconsistent.

Failure of the ultrafine sample to exceed the coarse sample in strength is declared falsifying, although sufficiently fine grains under the claimed inverse Hall-Petch regime could themselves be expected to weaken. The experiment does not specify where either sample lies relative to the critical grain size.
